strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: extending Laplacian-like diffusion smoothing to unstructured/irregular geometric data (point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures) without requiring mesh connectivity or manifold assumptions.

Provides a clean axiomatic framework (Laplace-like operators, diffusion operators, smoothing operators, Definitions 4.1-4.3) that clarifies how classical constructions (row/symmetric normalization, spectral truncation) fail to jointly satisfy mass conservation, symmetry, and positivity, motivating the proposed symmetric Sinkhorn normalization.

Solid theoretical grounding: proofs (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and supplementary appendices A-C) connect the construction to entropy-regularized optimal transport and rigorously establish symmetry, mass preservation, spectral damping in [0,1], and convergence as sample resolution increases, including a careful extension of the Metzler/Kato positivity condition to infinite-dimensional operators via semigroup theory.

Efficient, GPU-friendly, black-box algorithm (Algorithm 1) requiring only matrix-vector products, with fast empirical convergence (5-10 iterations) and scalable implementations via KeOps/attention-style formulations, applicable uniformly across data modalities.

Reasonably broad demonstration of versatility: spectral shape analysis/eigenvector approximation, gradient-flow preconditioning (Energy Distance descent), LDDMM-based shape interpolation robust to large deformations and topology changes, and integration into a learned correspondence pipeline (Q-DiffNet/ULRSSM).

Extensive supplementary material with additional qualitative validation across multiple shapes (sphere, cube, Armadillo) and representations (meshes, tetrahedra, point clouds, voxels, Gaussian mixtures), supporting reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is thin relative to the number of claimed applications: most results (spectral comparison, gradient flow, shape interpolation) are qualitative/visual rather than accompanied by numerical error metrics (e.g., no quantitative eigenvalue/eigenvector approximation error against the reference Laplacian beyond spectrum plots).

The one clearly quantitative experiment (Q-DiffNet shape correspondence, Figure 6) shows only mixed/modest improvements—competitive but not uniformly better than baselines on FAUST/SCAPE, with gains only clearly demonstrated on SHREC19—limiting the strength of the significance claim.

No runtime/scalability benchmarks are reported (the authors explicitly state they "do not report run times"), despite efficiency being a stated contribution, making it hard to assess practical scalability claims to millions of points.

The convergence theorem (4.2) only guarantees convergence of the discrete operator to a fixed-kernel-scale continuous operator Q, not to the true manifold Laplacian as σ→0, so the claim that the method "approximates" Laplacian behavior is asymptotically weaker than typical manifold-learning guarantees—an honestly disclosed but nonetheless real limitation.

The authors themselves describe the experiments as "preliminary," and the paper lacks ablations on sensitivity to key hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth σ, sample/resolution density, regularization ε) beyond a few illustrative appendix figures.

Presentation relies heavily on the appendix for essential technical and experimental details (proofs, dataset/mass-estimation specifics, hyperparameters), which could hinder self-contained understanding of the main paper.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: extends Laplacian-like heat diffusion to general unstructured data (point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures) without requiring explicit connectivity or manifold structure, which is a genuine gap in geometry processing.

Clean axiomatic framework (Definitions 4.1-4.3) that clarifies the shared structure of Laplacians, diffusion operators, and smoothing operators, and shows how row/symmetric/spectral normalizations are special cases with specific deficiencies (Fig. 2).

Solid theoretical grounding: Theorem 4.1 (existence/uniqueness of the symmetric Sinkhorn normalization) and Theorem 4.2 (convergence for Gaussian/exponential kernels as sample size grows) are proven rigorously in the appendix, connecting to entropic optimal transport theory (Knight & Ruiz; Feydy et al.).
Practical, GPU-friendly Algorithm 1 with fast empirical convergence (5-10 iterations), demonstrated to be compatible with KeOps/attention-style implementations for scalability to large point sets.

Reasonably broad qualitative demonstration across modalities (meshes, tetrahedra, point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids) and applications (spectral analysis, gradient flow smoothing, LDDMM geodesic interpolation, shape correspondence), with extensive supplementary figures (spheres, cubes, Armadillo) showing consistency of the eigenbasis across representations.
weaknesses: The paper's own conclusion admits the experiments "remain preliminary," and this is reflected in the results: most demonstrations (Figs. 1, 3-5, 7-17) are single-shape, qualitative illustrations rather than systematic quantitative evaluations with statistical rigor (no repeated trials, variance, or significance testing anywhere).

The one clear quantitative benchmark (Fig. 6a, shape correspondence) shows mixed and largely unfavorable results: Q-DiffNet underperforms DiffNet/ULRSSM on FAUST (2.5/2.1 vs 1.6/1.6) and SCAPE (3.1/2.4 vs 2.2/2.1), and only outperforms on S19 relative to point-cloud baselines while still losing to mesh-based methods (4.1/4.6 vs 3.5). This undercuts the significance claim that the operator is broadly useful as a "geometry-aware module."

Theorem 4.2 only establishes convergence of the normalized operator to a fixed-kernel continuous operator Q as sample resolution increases; the authors explicitly state they do NOT prove convergence to the true manifold Laplacian as sigma to 0, which is precisely the property motivating the framework's connection to differential-geometric Laplacians. This leaves an important theoretical gap unaddressed.

The volumetric vs. FEM eigenvalue comparison (Fig. 3) diverges starting around index ~20, indicating the spectral fidelity of the proposed operator is limited to low frequencies; this limitation is only briefly mentioned and not analyzed further, despite spectral fidelity being central to the paper's motivation (shape descriptors, functional maps often need more than 20 eigenvectors).

No runtime or scalability numbers are reported anywhere (explicitly stated in the supplementary: "we do not report run times"), despite an efficient, GPU-friendly algorithm being listed as a core contribution; this makes the efficiency claims unverifiable.

The Q-DiffNet point-cloud correspondence experiment still relies on mesh-derived WKS descriptors as network input even for the point-cloud variant, undermining the claim of applicability to genuinely unstructured/connectivity-free data, since ground-truth mesh structure is used to construct the descriptors that feed the network.

The core methodological device (symmetric/bistochastic Sinkhorn normalization of a similarity matrix) is adapted fairly directly from existing manifold-learning and optimal-transport literature (Knight & Ruiz 2014; Feydy et al. 2019; Cheng & Landa 2024; Wormell & Reich 2022); the novelty lies mainly in applying/axiomatizing this known technique for geometry-processing use cases rather than in a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical mechanism.

No direct empirical comparison against other recent nonmanifold/point-cloud Laplacian constructions (e.g., Sharp & Crane's nonmanifold Laplacian, winding-number-based point cloud Laplacians) that are discussed in related work but never benchmarked against, making it hard to assess whether the proposed approach offers practical advantages over existing alternatives designed for the same irregular-data setting.

strengths: Presents a clean, well-motivated algebraic framework (smoothing operators, Laplacian-like operators, diffusion operators) that unifies classical constructions (row, symmetric, spectral normalization) as special cases, clarifying assumptions that are often left implicit in the geometry-processing literature.

The core theoretical contribution—symmetric Sinkhorn normalization of a similarity/adjacency matrix with respect to a mass-weighted inner product—is rigorously justified: Theorem 4.1 is proven via a clean optimal-transport argument (entropy-regularized OT dual), and the extension of the Metzler/Kato positivity condition to infinite-dimensional L^2 spaces (Appendix A) is a nice technical addition that strengthens the connection to continuous heat semigroups.

Broad applicability across heterogeneous discrete representations (point clouds, sparse voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures, binary masks) is demonstrated with a single, GPU-friendly algorithm requiring only black-box matrix-vector products (Algorithm 1), with an elegant reformulation as an attention-style operator compatible with FlashAttention/xFormers.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a mostly theoretical paper: spectral comparison against FEM/cotangent Laplacians on multiple shapes and representations (Fig. 3, 8-14), a gradient-flow stabilization experiment (Fig. 4, 15-17), LDDMM shape interpolation showing qualitative improvement over raw kernel geodesics (Fig. 5), and a downstream, quantitative 3D shape-correspondence task (Q-DiffNet within ULRSSM) where the proposed operator is competitive with, and sometimes better than, established DiffusionNet/ULRSSM baselines on point-cloud inputs (Fig. 6).

Good reproducibility effort: detailed algorithmic descriptions, explicit convergence diagnostics for the Sinkhorn loop (Fig. 7), full derivations in a lengthy supplementary material, and clearly documented experimental setups (datasets, hyperparameters, training details) for each experiment.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly acknowledges that its experiments are 'preliminary,' and the downstream shape-matching results bear this out: Q-DiffNet does not clearly outperform mesh-based or even point-cloud baselines on FAUST/SCAPE (Fig. 6a), with gains confined to the more challenging SHREC19 set; the practical benefit of the method over existing heat-diffusion approximations is therefore only partially established.

Theorem 4.2 provides pointwise/uniform convergence of the normalized operator under a fixed kernel scale sigma as sample size grows, but the authors themselves note they do not prove convergence to the true manifold Laplacian as sigma -> 0, nor convergence of eigenvalues—leaving an important theoretical gap relative to prior bi-stochastic-Laplacian convergence results (e.g., Wormell & Reich; Cheng & Landa) that the paper otherwise builds on.

No runtime/scalability numbers are reported anywhere in the main text or supplement ('we do not report run times'), which undercuts the paper's repeated claims of GPU-efficiency and scalability, especially given the explicit future-work note that scalability 'can be further improved' for large point clouds/volumetric data.

Empirical comparisons to closely related normalization schemes discussed in the related work (e.g., bi-stochastically normalized graph Laplacians of Cheng & Landa, or Marshall & Coifman's manifold-learning bi-stochastic kernels) are largely theoretical/qualitative rather than direct quantitative baselines in the experiments section.

Several practical design choices (e.g., the heuristic eigenvalue-estimation formulas in Appendix E, the choice of m=2 diffusion applications in Q-DiffNet, kernel bandwidth sigma) are introduced somewhat ad hoc without systematic sensitivity analysis, leaving open how robust the method is to these hyperparameters in practice.

The shape-correspondence and LDDMM experiments are conducted on relatively small, well-studied human-body/anatomical benchmarks; it remains unclear how well the framework scales to noisier, larger, or more topologically diverse real-world data (e.g., raw LiDAR scans, large-scale Gaussian splats) that motivate the paper's introduction.

strengths: Provides a clean and well-motivated axiomatic framework (Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators) that unifies existing normalization schemes (row, symmetric, spectral) and clarifies their trade-offs regarding symmetry and mass conservation.

The core algorithmic contribution—symmetric Sinkhorn normalization of arbitrary smoothing kernels into diffusion-like operators—is simple, GPU-friendly, requires only matrix-vector products (no factorization), and is broadly applicable across heterogeneous discretizations (point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids, graphs).

Theoretical results (existence/uniqueness of the normalization, stability under increasing sampling density at fixed bandwidth, and robustness to mass-matrix perturbation) are proven rigorously in the appendix using established entropic-OT machinery (Feydy et al.), giving reasonable soundness to the central claims.

Extensive empirical validation: spectral consistency across modalities (Fig. 3, and additional shapes in appendix), stability to sampling density and bandwidth perturbations, gradient-flow stabilization for the Energy Distance, LDDMM geodesic regularization, and a shape-correspondence pipeline (Q-DiffNet) integrated into a competitive baseline (ULRSSM).

Honest and clearly articulated limitations section covering mass-matrix dependence, trade-offs of strict mass preservation, and weaker theoretical guarantees on convergence to a 'true' Laplacian for unstructured data.

Good positioning relative to prior diffusion-maps/manifold-learning literature, explicitly distinguishing the fixed-scale geometry-processing goal from the asymptotic N→∞, σ→0 regime studied by Wormell & Reich and Cheng & Landa.
weaknesses: The central theoretical machinery (symmetric Sinkhorn scaling via entropic optimal transport duals) is largely a direct application of existing results (Knight et al. 2014; Feydy et al. 2019); the paper's novelty lies more in framing/application to geometry processing than in fundamentally new mathematics, which somewhat limits the originality claim.

The shape-correspondence experiment (Table 2), presented as a flagship application, shows mixed results: Q-DiffNet underperforms mesh-based and even some point-cloud baselines on FAUST/SCAPE, and the reported SHREC19 gains are not clearly disentangled from other confounds (e.g., partial-data robustness, use of mesh-derived WKS features shared across all methods) rather than isolating the specific benefit of the proposed operator.

The runtime comparison (Table 1) contrasts GPU Sinkhorn iterations against CPU sparse LU factorization for implicit Laplacian diffusion, which is an apples-to-oranges comparison (different hardware, different algorithmic classes); a fair comparison (e.g., GPU sparse solvers or CPU Sinkhorn vs CPU Laplacian, as later partially done in the appendix) would better support efficiency claims made in the main text.

Some qualitative demonstrations (Figures 4, 5, and their extensions) are illustrative rather than rigorously quantified in the main paper (quantitative metrics like Chamfer distance or area distortion are relegated to the appendix), which weakens the persuasiveness of these use cases as standalone evidence in the main text.

Dependence on an accurate mass matrix M is acknowledged as a limitation, but in practice for genuinely irregular real-world data (e.g., noisy captured point clouds or splats) mass estimation itself may be nontrivial and this is not stress-tested beyond synthetic perturbation experiments on a single mesh.
The claim of 'state of the art shape correspondence on unstructured data' in the abstract/intro appears overstated relative to the actual mixed quantitative results in Table 2.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem: extending heat-diffusion-like smoothing to unstructured domains (point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids, splats) where no principled Laplacian is readily available.

Solid theoretical framework: the paper carefully axiomatizes Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators (Defs 4.1-4.3), proves existence/uniqueness of the symmetric Sinkhorn normalization (Thm 4.4), establishes convergence under mesh/point refinement at fixed bandwidth (Thm 4.5), and derives a quantitative stability bound to mass-matrix perturbation (Prop 4.6), connecting cleanly to entropic optimal transport theory (Feydy et al., Knight et al.).

Broad empirical scope: the method is instantiated and visually/quantitatively validated across many representations (meshes, point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids) with consistent spectral behavior relative to the FEM/cotangent Laplacian (Fig. 3, extensive appendix figures on sphere/cube/horse/armadillo).

Practical relevance demonstrated through multiple applications: gradient-flow stabilization (Energy Distance minimization), LDDMM-style geodesic shooting with improved extrapolation behavior, and integration into a learned shape-correspondence pipeline (Q-DiffNet/ULRSSM).

Good attention to reproducibility and implementation: efficient GPU-friendly formulation (reduction to attention-style softmax), runtime benchmarking against sparse Laplacian solvers, and extensive supplementary experiments on convergence rate, robustness to non-uniform sampling, and bandwidth sensitivity.
The paper is honest about limitations (dependence on the mass matrix, strict mass preservation trade-offs, weaker theoretical guarantees for unstructured data) rather than overselling universality.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic contribution is largely a direct application of pre-existing symmetric Sinkhorn/entropic-OT machinery (Knight et al., 2014; Feydy et al., 2019) to the geometry-processing setting; the proofs in the appendix lean heavily on quoting results from Feydy et al. (2019) rather than developing substantially new machinery, which somewhat limits methodological originality relative to the claims made in the introduction.

The downstream shape-correspondence experiment (Table 2), which is presented as a flagship demonstration of 'state of the art' performance, is mixed: Q-DiffNet underperforms mesh-based upper bounds on FAUST and SCAPE, the Q-FM fully-Laplacian-free variant performs noticeably worse, and the strict point-based ablation (Table 4, XYZ-only inputs) shows substantially degraded and less clearly superior performance for all methods, undercutting the 'state of the art' framing in the abstract/contributions.

No direct empirical comparison against the closely related bi-stochastic/manifold-learning normalization baselines discussed at length in Related Work (e.g., Marshall & Coifman, Wormell & Reich, Cheng & Landa) on any of the main tasks, despite these being the most natural competing normalization schemes.

The runtime comparison (Table 1) contrasts a GPU brute-force Sinkhorn with a CPU sparse LU solve, which is somewhat favorable framing; a more balanced comparison (e.g., against GPU-capable approximate/implicit diffusion or iterative Laplacian solvers) would better establish the claimed practical efficiency advantage.

Essentially all technical substance (proofs, implementation details, most experiments) is relegated to a lengthy appendix (sections A-J), leaving the 9-page main body as largely descriptive scaffolding; this reduces self-containedness and makes it harder to assess core claims without consulting ~20 pages of supplementary material.

The positivity/PSD assumptions needed for the spectral bound (property iii, relying on K being positive semi-definite) are somewhat restrictive and not deeply discussed in terms of which practical similarity/adjacency matrices actually satisfy them beyond Gaussian-type kernels.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: extending heat-diffusion-like smoothing to unstructured geometric data (point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids) where no explicit Laplacian/connectivity is available.

A clean axiomatic framework (Laplace-like operators, diffusion operators, smoothing operators) clarifies how classical normalization schemes (row, symmetric, spectral truncation) relate to and fall short of the proposed symmetric Sinkhorn normalization, which simultaneously achieves symmetry and mass preservation.

The theoretical contributions are solid and carefully proved: existence/uniqueness of the symmetric Sinkhorn scaling via entropic optimal transport duality (Theorem 4.4), convergence under sample refinement at fixed bandwidth (Theorem 4.5, distinguishing this work from the asymptotic manifold-learning literature), and a first-order stability bound to mass-matrix perturbation (Proposition 4.6), which is also validated empirically.

The method is simple to implement, GPU-friendly, requires only black-box matrix-vector products, and the authors show an elegant reformulation as an attention-style kernel compatible with FlashAttention/xFormers, which is practically appealing.

Broad empirical demonstration across diverse representations (meshes, point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids) with consistent spectral behavior relative to FEM Laplacian references (Figure 3 and extensive appendix material with spheres, cubes, additional animal shapes, and robustness studies to sampling density/bandwidth).

Diverse and meaningful downstream applications: gradient flow stabilization in Wasserstein-type particle dynamics, LDDMM-based geodesic shape interpolation/extrapolation showing qualitatively more plausible paths than standard Gaussian-kernel LDDMM, and integration into a state-of-the-art shape matching pipeline (ULRSSM/DiffusionNet) with competitive or superior results on SHREC19.

The limitations section is honest and specific (dependence on mass matrix quality, strict mass preservation potentially limiting expressivity, lack of guaranteed convergence to a 'true' continuous Laplacian on fully unstructured data), rather than being generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The shape-matching results in Table 2 are somewhat uneven and not fully convincing: Q-DiffNet clearly underperforms mesh-based baselines on FAUST/SCAPE while outperforming them on SHREC19; no variance/error bars or multiple training seeds are reported, making it hard to assess whether the SHREC19 improvement is robust or due to run-to-run variability.

The GPU-vs-CPU runtime comparison (Table 1) contrasts Sinkhorn on GPU with sparse LU factorization on CPU, which is a somewhat uneven comparison (different hardware and different amortization assumptions); although the authors acknowledge this, it limits the strength of the scalability claims relative to a more controlled comparison (e.g., GPU sparse solvers or CPU Sinkhorn with equivalent precomputation).

While the axiomatic synthesis is useful, the core technical machinery (symmetric Sinkhorn scaling, entropic optimal-transport duality, convergence results) builds closely on existing work (Knight et al. 2014; Feydy et al. 2019; Wormell & Reich 2021; Cheng & Landa 2024), so the methodological novelty is more in framing/application to geometry processing at fixed scale than in a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

Several applications (e.g., pose interpolation in Figure 5/20, gradient flow experiments) are primarily qualitative/illustrative with limited quantitative benchmarking beyond a single area-distortion plot or Chamfer distance curve, limiting the strength of the claimed practical benefits.

No principled guidance is given for choosing the bandwidth σ in different applications; sensitivity analyses exist in the appendix but remain largely empirical/qualitative rather than offering actionable selection criteria.

Scalability at very large sizes (millions of points) still requires several seconds per normalization on a V100, and the dense/kernel-based approach may not match the efficiency of mature sparse factorization methods when a high-quality mesh Laplacian is actually available, somewhat narrowing the practical scope of the speed argument.
